content: 1. Ensure that areas where prosthetics and orthotics are fabricated are separated from noisier, dustier activities typically associated with workshops. 2. Maintain cleanliness, organization, and tidiness in all areas, including assembly and machine rooms. 3. Verify that all personnel interacting with users are adequately trained and competent in their roles. 4. Implement a user policy to ensure services are user-oriented and sensitive to gender considerations. 5. Encourage all personnel in contact with users to wear clinical uniforms and name badges for easy identification. 6. Adhere to appropriate dress codes, especially when representing services in interactions with government agencies or offices. 7. Use professional terminology when referring to prosthetics and orthotics units, such as departments, clinics, laboratories, or centres, rather than workshops or limb-fitting centres, to avoid reducing the perception of the field to mere technical work. 8. The term prosthetics and orthotics workshop should only be used to describe the specific area where devices are fabricated. 9. Use terms like prostheses and orthoses or prosthetic and orthotic products instead of outdated terms like caliper or appliance. 10. Appropriate technology in prosthetics and orthotics is defined as a system that provides proper fit and alignment tailored to the individual’s needs while being sustainable and cost-effective for the country. 11. Proper fit and alignment must be based on sound biomechanical principles. 12. The appropriateness of technologies, components, materials, and methods should be evaluated based on user acceptability, economic feasibility, and technical suitability. 13. Cost-effectiveness in prosthetics and orthotics services is heavily influenced by the choice of technology, components, and materials. 14. Continuous market research is essential to identify cost-effective options while ensuring quality, durability, and availability. 15. Multiple technologies of varying sophistication and price levels can be used simultaneously to meet diverse needs. 16. Any technology that is requested, paid for, and does not restrict access to services can be considered appropriate, including advanced and expensive products for users with the financial means or insurance coverage to afford them. 17. Prosthetic and orthotic products should generally suit the user’s needs, be culturally appropriate, and respect individual lifestyles, such as walking barefoot or sitting cross-legged. 18. Products should be suitable for the local climate, terrain, and working conditions. 19. Products must be affordable for both the system and the individual, cost-effective, and promote sustainable development by utilizing local markets and materials. 20. Technologies and methods should adhere to international standards, ensure biomechanically correct products, and be durable with a long lifespan. 21. Products should be easy to adjust, maintain, and repair, ideally by the users themselves. 22. Prosthetists and orthotists must have sufficient skills and knowledge to apply technologies effectively, with training provided if necessary. 23. Working methods should not pose hazards to personnel, and materials should be easy to store. 24. Prosthetic and orthotic products should be comfortable, functional, and meet the same quality requirements regardless of the product level. 25. Service providers should ideally offer a full range of products to meet diverse user needs and preferences. 26. Basic prosthetic and orthotic products provide essential functions and comfort, are made from lightweight materials like thermoplastics, steel, or aluminum, and are relatively low-cost. 27. Intermediate products use a wider range of materials, such as thermoplastics, composites, and metals, and may include more advanced components like articulated joints or hydraulic systems. 28. Advanced products incorporate smart controls and materials that detect user movements, such as microprocessor-controlled knees or myoelectric hands. 29. Advanced products require higher expertise and are more expensive, but some manufacturers are reducing costs to make them accessible in low-income settings. 30. 3D printing offers a cleaner, faster, and less invasive method for fabricating prosthetics and orthotics, especially for children. 31. 3D scanning captures body dimensions to create digital models for printing custom devices or components. 32. While 3D printing has advantages, it is not universally applicable, and clinicians must understand its benefits compared to conventional methods. 33. Specialized training is essential when introducing new products, components, or methods to ensure safety, maximize potential, and protect financial investments. 34. Prefabricated products, such as certain orthoses, are available in various sizes and can be selected based on clinical criteria. 35. Prefabricated products are often less expensive and allow faster fitting but may be less effective than custom-made devices. 36. Custom-made products are chosen when a closer fit, better function, or stronger support is required. 37. Custom-made devices are constructed from a wide range of materials and require detailed body measurements and modeling. 38. WHO estimates that over one billion people need assistive products for mobility, vision, hearing, communication, or cognition. 39. To improve access to affordable, high-quality assistive products, WHO’s GATE initiative developed a priority assistive products list in consultation with experts, users, and caregivers.
